title: Legislative Framework, Ethics and Business Principles

lessons.title: The laws that shape a South African farm
lessons.html:
Why a farmer must know the law

A mixed crop and livestock farm is a workplace, a food producer, a water user and a land manager at the same time. Each of these roles is governed by legislation. As a farm supervisor or manager you do not need to be a lawyer, but you must know which laws apply, what they expect of the farm, and when to ask for specialist advice.

Labour and employment

  • Basic Conditions of Employment Act 75 of 1997 and the Sectoral Determination for the Farm Worker Sector: working hours, overtime, leave, written particulars of employment and payslips.
  • National Minimum Wage Act 9 of 2018: farm workers are covered by the national minimum wage. Check the current rate each year when it is adjusted.
  • Labour Relations Act 66 of 1995: fair dismissal, disciplinary procedures, the right to join a trade union, and the CCMA for disputes.
  • Employment Equity Act 55 of 1998: no unfair discrimination in hiring, pay or promotion.
  • Unemployment Insurance Act 63 of 2001 and the Compensation for Occupational Injuries and Diseases Act 130 of 1993 (COIDA): register workers for UIF and with the Compensation Fund.

Safety, animals and chemicals

  • Occupational Health and Safety Act 85 of 1993: the employer must provide a safe workplace, training, protective equipment and safe machinery.
  • Fertilizers, Farm Feeds, Agricultural Remedies and Stock Remedies Act 36 of 1947: only registered products may be used, and the label is a legal instruction.
  • Animals Protection Act 71 of 1962: cruelty, neglect and unnecessary suffering are offences.
  • Animal Diseases Act 35 of 1984: controlled diseases must be reported and movement restrictions obeyed.

Land and natural resources

  • Conservation of Agricultural Resources Act 43 of 1983: protects soil, vleis and veld, and controls declared weeds and invader plants.
  • National Water Act 36 of 1998: water use, such as irrigation from a river or borehole above certain limits, may need registration or a licence.
  • Extension of Security of Tenure Act 62 of 1997 (ESTA): protects the rights of people living on farms; evictions must follow the legal process.

Laws change. Keep a register of the laws that apply to your farm, note who is responsible for each, and check for updates through your organised agriculture body, the Department of Agriculture or a labour consultant.

lessons.title: Ethics on the farm
lessons.html:
Doing the right thing when nobody is watching

Legislation sets the minimum. Ethics is about how the farm behaves beyond the minimum: honesty, fairness, respect and responsibility. Buyers, banks, workers and the community all judge a farm on its ethics, and a damaged reputation is very hard to repair.

Ethics towards workers

  • Pay correctly and on time, with a clear payslip. Never make unlawful deductions.
  • Treat everyone with respect. No shouting, insults or favouritism.
  • Apply rules and discipline consistently to everyone.
  • Respect the housing and tenure rights of farm dwellers.

Ethics towards customers and the public

  • Never sell produce or animals still within a chemical or medicine withdrawal period.
  • Describe grade, weight and origin honestly. Do not mix poor product into a good load.
  • Keep accurate spray, treatment and traceability records.

Ethics towards animals and the environment

  • Handle livestock calmly and treat sick or injured animals promptly.
  • Do not over-graze, pollute rivers or dump chemical containers.
  • Respect neighbours: control fires, fences, stray animals and spray drift.

Handling an ethical problem

Suppose a buyer offers you R2 000 in cash to load his trucks first and give him the best-grade maize. This is a bribe and a conflict of interest. A simple test helps: Is it legal? Is it fair to everyone involved? Would I be comfortable if the owner, my workers or the newspaper knew about it? If any answer is no, do not do it. Refuse politely, record what happened, and report it to the farm owner or manager.

A written code of conduct, explained to all staff in a language they understand, makes expectations clear. It should cover honesty, gifts, use of farm property, harassment and how to report concerns without fear of victimisation.

lessons.title: Business principles for the mixed farm
lessons.html:
Running the farm as a business

A farm only survives if, over time, income is greater than costs. Good farming practice must be matched by good business practice.

Forms of business

FormMain feature
Sole proprietorSimple to start; the owner is personally liable for all debts.
PartnershipTwo or more owners share profits and are personally liable.
Private company (Pty) LtdRegistered under the Companies Act 71 of 2008 with CIPC; a separate legal person with limited liability.
Co-operativeMembers jointly own and control the business, often for shared buying, marketing or equipment.

Core business tools

  • Enterprise budget: estimate income and costs for each enterprise, for example 20 ha of maize or a herd of 60 Bonsmara cows.
  • Gross margin: gross income minus directly allocated (variable) costs such as seed, fertiliser, feed, dip and vet costs. It lets you compare enterprises.
  • Cash-flow budget: shows month by month when money comes in and goes out. Crops often pay only once a year, so you must plan for the months of no income.
  • Records: invoices, receipts, stock registers and bank statements support tax returns and loan applications.

Worked example

A weaner calf enterprise sells 40 calves at an average of R7 500 each, giving R300 000 gross income. Variable costs (supplementary feed, licks, vaccines, dipping, transport and commission) total R140 000. The gross margin is R160 000. Fixed costs such as permanent wages, insurance and fencing repairs must still be paid from this margin before there is any profit.

Tax and compliance

The business must be registered with SARS for income tax, and for VAT if turnover passes the compulsory registration threshold. Employers must also register for PAYE, UIF and the skills development levy where they apply. Use a registered accountant or tax practitioner when you are unsure.

Key points

  • Labour, safety, animal, chemical, land and water laws all apply to a mixed farm.
  • The product label is a legal instruction under Act 36 of 1947.
  • Ethics goes beyond the law: honesty, fairness and respect protect the farm's reputation.
  • Use enterprise budgets, gross margins and cash-flow budgets to manage the business.
  • Keep complete records for SARS, the bank and your buyers.
